question: I want quality — companies that are really good at making profit from what they own, cheap-ish, growing, and not drowning in debt. Give me a few.

_conventions._note: For the fields below, read the `definition` and/or `sign` before interpreting the value — a negative can MEAN something (an outflow, a benefit) and an ambiguous name needs its definition. Every other field is a plain magnitude.

eps_diluted.definition: PER SHARE, in the company's REPORTING currency (NOT USD-normalized like the _usd fields) — don't mix it with the USD amounts.

total_debt.definition: Short + long-term borrowings + finance leases (operating leases excluded) — the Bloomberg/CapIQ 'Total Debt' basis. Borrowings-only = current_debt + long_term_debt.

answer_to_user: Here's a short list that tries to hit ALL four of your 'quality' tests at once — good at turning what they own into profit (high return on equity, above peer average), reasonably-priced (P/E below the peer average), growing revenue each year, and not loaded with debt. Names that cleared every filter include Alphabet/Google (GOOG), Amazon (AMZN), Meta (META), Tencent (0700.HK), Chubb (CB), Progressive (PGR) and PDD Holdings (PDD). Why they qualify as 'quality': e.g. Alphabet combines a fat ~55% net margin, huge free cash flow, tiny debt and a below-average ~17x P/E; Meta and Amazon show strong margins and low leverage with steady growth; the insurers (Chubb, Progressive) are steady, profitable and reasonably valued. A trade-off to be honest about: it's rare for a company to be top-tier on profitability AND growth AND cheap AND debt-free — usually something gives, so treat 'cheap-ish' as relative to peers rather than an outright bargain. Informational only — not a recommendation to buy, and figures are the companies' real reported numbers.
